Policy Name/Number: AB1979 – AI Clinical Decision Support and Healthcare Chatbot Confidentiality
Summary: Preserves licensed clinical judgment, prohibits autonomous performance of licensed clinical functions, and extends medical-information confidentiality law to qualifying consumer healthcare chatbots.
Healthcare Implications: Covered care settings must preserve professional judgment when using clinical AI. Routine nonjudgment documentation is excluded; supervised trainees remain permitted. Chatbot businesses gain confidentiality duties.
Keyword Tags: Safety & Risk; Clinical Quality & Efficacy; Privacy & Data; Transparency & Governance
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: H1: AI may not perform reserved clinical functions (diagnosis, treatment decisions, prescribing, formal clinical assessment) without licensed professional involvement.
Specific Implications: Covered facilities and practices may not deploy AI to independently perform licensed clinical functions or direct unlicensed staff to perform them; supervised training and nonjudgment administrative uses are excepted.

Policy Name/Number: SB503 – Clinical Decision Support Systems: Bias and Documentation
Summary: Requires developers and deployers to identify foreseeable clinical decision-support bias risks, developers to mitigate risks and provide documentation, and deployers to monitor and mitigate biased impacts.
Healthcare Implications: Healthcare organizations must evaluate bias risks and monitor covered clinical AI. Vendor documentation is due upon request or initial sale, whichever comes first, and material updates; a limited internal-development documentation exception applies.
Keyword Tags: Equity & Bias; Transparency & Governance; Safety & Risk; Clinical Quality & Efficacy
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: E1: AI systems must be evaluated for discriminatory or biased outcomes; entities must take specified action if discrimination is found. | P1: Internal procedures (impact assessments, periodic reviews, training) the deploying entity must maintain.
Specific Implications: Developers and deployers must reasonably identify foreseeable bias risks; developers must reasonably mitigate them and deployers take proportionate mitigation steps. | Deployers must regularly monitor identified clinical decision-support systems for biased impacts; no fixed monitoring interval is specified.

Policy Name/Number: AB1609 – Customer Service Chatbots and Pharmacy Human Contact
Summary: Requires covered large private businesses to identify misleadingly human-like customer-service chatbots and provide human-contact options. An express pharmacy provision permits a return call within one business hour. Hospital communications about healthcare delivery, administration and payment are exempt.
Healthcare Implications: Applies to covered pharmacies and other nonexempt businesses above $500 million national revenue. The pharmacy-specific handoff provision provides a defined healthcare nexus; this is customer-service governance, with no clinical decision-review right.
Stakeholder Tags: Patients & Public; Providers & Health Systems; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: D1: AI systems must disclose their non-human nature when interacting directly with users.
Specific Implications: Covered businesses must not represent a customer-service chatbot as human and must disclose its artificial nature in the interaction medium when a reasonable person would be misled; hospital healthcare communications are exempt.

Policy Name/Number: SB1119 – Adam’s Law
Summary: Creates child-chatbot safety obligations and replaces SB243’s original minor provisions. Core new duties begin July 1, 2027; audit deadlines are phased.
Healthcare Implications: Covered operators must address psychological harm and crisis response. Child diagnosis or treatment is restricted to purpose-designed, FDA-regulated, HIPAA-compliant medical devices.
Keyword Tags: Safety & Risk; Transparency & Governance; Privacy & Data; Clinical Quality & Efficacy
Stakeholder Tags: Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government

Policy Name/Number: HB380 – Personal Data Privacy Act Amendments: Automated Decisions
Summary: Amends Delaware’s privacy law to expand protections for automated decisions, expressly including decisions about access to health-care services. Adds contractual safeguards for third-party decision reports, including adverse-action notices and notice of qualified human-review rights, and strengthens protections for sensitive data.
Healthcare Implications: Covered organizations using personal data for automated health-care access decisions must assess applicable opt-out, notice, and human-review requirements. Coverage is limited: insurers and health carriers are exempt, as are HIPAA-protected health information and specified other clinical data. The law does not impose a blanket human-review requirement on clinical AI or insurance decisions.
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: PR2: Individuals affected by consequential AI-driven decisions have the right to request human review. | P1: Internal procedures (impact assessments, periodic reviews, training) the deploying entity must maintain.
Specific Implications: For covered third-party decision reports, require contractual adverse-action notice and notice of a right to request human review where technically feasible, subject to the resident’s-best-interest exception; expands automated-decision opt-out rights. | Covered controllers must assess qualifying risky profiling; the data-protection-assessment threshold is 50,000 consumers.

Policy Name/Number: SB3001 – Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and Safety Act
Summary: Requires AI-companion operators to disclose when users are interacting with AI; adopt evidence-based suicide and self-harm response protocols; avoid representing companions as professional mental or behavioral health care; implement safeguards against outputs encouraging serious bodily injury; and provide specified protections for known minors. Beginning January 1, 2028, operators must report crisis-referral and protocol information annually to the Department of Health. Violations are unfair or deceptive acts or practices.
Healthcare Implications: Creates binding safeguards for companion systems used for emotional support or mental-health-adjacent interactions. Operators must implement crisis-referral, evidence-based self-harm assessment, youth-safety, disclosure, and reporting workflows; the Department of Health gains oversight information, while the law creates no private right of action.
Keyword Tags: Safety & Risk; Transparency & Governance; Clinical Quality & Efficacy
Stakeholder Tags: Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government

Specific Implications: Operators must clearly and conspicuously notify users that an AI companion is not human when a reasonable person could be misled; if the operator has actual knowledge or reasonable certainty that a user is a minor, it must provide a persistent disclaimer or a session-start disclosure with hourly reminders. | Operators may not cause or program an AI companion to represent that it is designed to provide professional mental or behavioral health care. | Operators must adopt protocols for suicidal ideation or self-harm, use evidence-based methods, refer users to crisis services, prevent human-like crisis representations, and restrict outputs that encourage serious bodily injury. | When the operator has actual knowledge or reasonable certainty that a user is a minor, it must restrict specified engagement-maximizing and sexual content, support parental controls, and apply enhanced disclosure reminders. | Beginning January 1, 2028, operators must submit annual reports to the Behavioral Health Administration of the Department of Health on crisis referrals and response protocols without including user-identifying information.

Policy Name/Number: SB3114 – Transparency in Downcoding Act
Summary: Prohibits health care payors from using algorithms or other automated tools that bypass provider-submitted information to downcode claims. Automated tools may flag claims, but every downcoding determination and dispute must be made or reviewed by a natural person; payors must provide reasons and a dispute process, may not downcode solely from diagnosis codes, and may not target clinicians who treat complex or chronic patients.
Healthcare Implications: Directly regulates AI-enabled claims adjudication across covered commercial, public-employee, Medicaid managed-care, and CHIP coverage. Payors must add human review, claim-specific clinical review, notice, dispute, and anti-discrimination controls and remain responsible for delegated vendors; the Department of Insurance and Department of Healthcare and Family Services enforce the requirements.
Keyword Tags: Safety & Risk; Transparency & Governance; Clinical Quality & Efficacy; Equity & Bias
Stakeholder Tags: Payers & Purchasers; Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Regulators & Government

Policy Name/Number: SB315 – Ohio Medicaid Program Integrity and Fraud Prevention Act: Automated Review
Summary: Requires automated checks for alternative primary insurance before Medicaid claims are paid. When the Department uses automated review tools for specified eligibility, claims and provider-integrity functions, an appropriate Department employee must review the findings before action. Directs rulemaking on insurance-discovery engines and processing.
Healthcare Implications: Ohio Medicaid and managed care claims workflows must screen for other primary coverage before payment. Covered Department decisions cannot take effect automatically from an AI or other automated tool; human review must confirm correctness. This is program-integrity governance, rather than a requirement for clinician review of medical necessity.
Stakeholder Tags: Payers & Purchasers; Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: H2: Consequential AI-driven decisions affecting individuals' rights, benefits, or welfare require human review before taking effect. | G2: Directs an agency to issue binding rules, standards, or regulatory guidance on AI.
Specific Implications: For the functions specified in R.C. 5162.90 and 5164.11, the Department of Medicaid must not act automatically on automated-review findings; the responsible Department employee must first review and confirm the determination. | The Department of Medicaid must adopt implementing rules for R.C. 5162.19, including standards for approved insurance-discovery engines, claims-processing timelines and reporting.

Policy Name/Number: HB30 / Chapter1, Item295 – Medicaid Call-Center AI Procurement
Summary: The 2026–2028 budget directs DMAS to seek AI opportunities in call-center operations and requires related contract procurements, re-procurements and modifications to maximize AI for cost and service improvements, while protecting personal information and complying with federal law.
Healthcare Implications: Directs AI adoption and contracting within Virginia Medicaid administration. Applies to DMAS call-center procurement and personal-information safeguards; it does not authorize automated eligibility or clinical decisions or create a human-review right.
Stakeholder Tags: Payers & Purchasers; Developers & Vendors; Patients & Public; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: None
Specific Implications: None

Policy Name/Number: S2197 – Oversight of Artificial Intelligence Technology in Mental Health Care Act
Summary: Restricts AI use in therapy and psychotherapy, including independent therapeutic decisions and treatment plans. Written notice and revocable consent apply to the specified emotionally engaging AI/companion uses in recorded or transcribed sessions. Excludes specified FDA/federally cleared tools and approved research, as well as religious counseling, peer support and public self-help resources.
Healthcare Implications: Therapy providers must preserve clinical judgment and reasonable oversight under the law’s relationship and consent conditions. The consent trigger is narrower than every AI-recorded session. FDA/federally cleared tools and qualifying research are excluded; providers are not made responsible for vendor-controlled design, algorithms or outputs.
Keyword Tags: Safety & Risk; Clinical Quality & Efficacy; Transparency & Governance; Privacy & Data
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government

Specific Implications: A licensed professional or provider may not allow AI to make independent therapeutic decisions, determine therapeutic recommendations or treatment plans, or directly interact with clients in therapeutic communication except under the law’s relationship, consent, and oversight conditions. | For AI designed to simulate emotional attachment, bonding or dependency, or AI companions for mental-health/emotional support, written notice of AI use and its purpose and revocable consent are required when assisting supplementary support or therapeutic communication in recorded/transcribed sessions, subject to statutory exclusions. | A person or entity may not provide, advertise, or offer therapy or psychotherapy services through AI unless the services are conducted by a licensed professional or provider. | The Executive Office of Health and Human Services may investigate suspected violations and promulgate rules to carry out the act.

Policy Name/Number: H7538 – Use of Artificial Intelligence by Healthcare Providers Notification Act
Summary: Requires healthcare providers and healthcare facilities that use artificial intelligence to document in-person or telehealth visits to notify patients of that AI use and review AI-generated documentation for accuracy after the visit.
Healthcare Implications: Directly affects ambient documentation, AI scribing, and other AI tools used to memorialize patient visits. Healthcare providers and facilities must notify patients when AI is used for visit documentation and remain responsible for reviewing the resulting documentation for accuracy.
Keyword Tags: Transparency & Governance; Clinical Quality & Efficacy; Safety & Risk
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government

Specific Implications: Healthcare providers and healthcare facilities using AI to document in-person or telehealth visits must notify patients that AI is being used for that purpose and review the AI-generated documentation for accuracy after the visit.

Policy Name/Number: S2195 – Artificial Intelligence Companion Models
Summary: Regulates operators of AI companion systems that use AI, generative AI, or emotional-recognition algorithms to simulate sustained human-like relationships with users. Requires covered AI companions to include protocols for suicidal ideation, self-harm, and possible physical harm to others, provide crisis-resource notifications when those expressions are detected, provide recurring disclosures that the user is not communicating with a human, and file annual safety-protocol reports with the Attorney General beginning July 1, 2027. Authorizes AG enforcement and civil penalties.
Healthcare Implications: Not healthcare-specific, but relevant to mental-health-adjacent AI companions and consumer AI systems that may interact with users expressing suicidality, self-harm, or emotional distress. Operators must implement crisis-response protocols, provide human/non-human disclosure, report safety-protocol metrics to the Attorney General, and face civil penalties for noncompliance.
Keyword Tags: Safety & Risk; Transparency & Governance; Clinical Quality & Efficacy
Stakeholder Tags: Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government

Specific Implications: Operators must provide a clear and conspicuous notification at the beginning of any AI companion interaction and at least every three hours during continuing interactions that the user is not communicating with a human. | Operators may not provide an AI companion unless it contains a protocol for possible suicidal ideation, self-harm, or physical harm to others and provides crisis-resource notifications as soon as those expressions are detected. | Beginning July 1, 2027, operators must file annual reports with the Attorney General that include the number of safety-protocol activations and related metrics; the Attorney General must publish aggregated data.

Policy Name/Number: H0816 – Regulating the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Provision of Mental Health Services
Summary: Prohibits corporations and entities from providing, advertising, or offering mental health services, including through artificial intelligence, unless the services are provided by a mental health professional or are part of an approved institutional review board or privacy board study. Allows mental health professionals to use HIPAA-compliant AI tools, including certain FDA-authorized software products, if the professional reviews and approves the mental health services. Makes prohibited AI use unprofessional conduct and requires the Artificial Intelligence Advisory Council to report on regulation of AI use by mental health professionals.
Healthcare Implications: Creates direct guardrails for AI use in mental and behavioral health services. AI systems may not independently provide mental health services to the public, and mental health professionals remain responsible for reviewing and approving AI-supported services. The law creates professional-discipline and consumer-protection consequences for prohibited AI use and sets up further legislative review of AI use by mental health professionals.
Keyword Tags: Safety & Risk; Clinical Quality & Efficacy; Transparency & Governance; Privacy & Data
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government

Specific Implications: Corporations and entities may not provide, advertise, or offer mental health services through AI unless the services are provided by a mental health professional or are part of an approved research study; mental health professionals may use HIPAA-compliant AI tools only if they review and approve the mental health services. | A corporation or entity may not present AI-delivered services as mental health services for the public unless the services are provided by a mental health professional or qualify under the approved-study exception. | By January 15, 2027, the Artificial Intelligence Advisory Council must submit a report to legislative committees on regulating AI use by mental health professionals, including recommendations for legislative action.

Policy Name/Number: S71 – Data Privacy and Online Surveillance
Summary: Creates profiling opt-out and explanation rights for consequential decisions, including healthcare services, and requires impact assessments. Privacy notices must disclose personal-data use for large-language-model training.
Healthcare Implications: Nonexempt health-related controllers face automated-decision rights and governance duties. Qualifying providers, facilities, insurers, third-party administrators, and protected health information have exemptions. The housing-only reevaluation right is not a general healthcare human-review right.
Stakeholder Tags: Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: P1: Internal procedures (impact assessments, periodic reviews, training) the deploying entity must maintain. | P2: Deploying entities must publicly disclose or file with regulators detailed information about their AI systems, policies, or inventories.
Specific Implications: Document impact assessments for consequential profiling; assessment requirements apply to processing created or generated after January 1, 2028. | Provide detailed consequential-profiling impact assessments to the Attorney General on request during an investigation; assessments are confidential.

Policy Name/Number: HB1195 – Psychotherapy Artificial Intelligence Restrictions
Summary: Restricts the use of artificial intelligence systems in psychotherapy services. Regulated psychotherapy professionals may use AI for administrative or supplementary support if they remain responsible for reviewing AI outputs and comply with privacy and security law. The law bars AI from therapeutic communication without real-time professional involvement, bars AI-generated therapeutic recommendations or treatment plans without professional review and approval, requires written informed consent before AI recording or transcription of therapeutic sessions, and prohibits misleading AI representations that imply psychotherapy services, professional endorsement, or confidentiality.
Healthcare Implications: Creates direct guardrails for AI use in mental and behavioral health care. Psychotherapy providers must keep human professional involvement in therapeutic workflows, obtain written consent before AI recording or transcription, review AI outputs used for clinical support, and prevent AI tools from being marketed or presented as substitutes for regulated psychotherapy services. Vendors and deployers of psychotherapy-related AI tools face consumer-protection and professional-discipline risk for misleading interfaces, advertising, or outputs.
Keyword Tags: Safety & Risk; Clinical Quality & Efficacy; Transparency & Governance; Privacy & Data
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government

Specific Implications: Regulated psychotherapy professionals may not allow AI to interact with clients in therapeutic communication without synchronous, real-time interaction among the professional, the AI system, and the client; AI may not generate therapeutic recommendations or treatment plans without professional review and approval, and may not provide, direct, or guide psychotherapy, clinical intervention, counseling, diagnosis, or treatment planning unless statutory conditions are satisfied. | Before using AI to record or transcribe a therapeutic session, the provider must inform the client or representative in writing that AI will be used and for what specific purposes, obtain written informed consent, and respect refusal or revocation without denying psychotherapy services. | A person may not provide, advertise, or offer psychotherapy services through AI unless the services are provided by a regulated professional, and may not use AI advertising, interface, or outputs to imply professional endorsement, equivalence to psychotherapy services, or confidentiality protections for user data.

Policy Name/Number: H8345 Substitute A – Digital Technology and Mental Health Study Commission
Summary: Creates a 14-member commission to study digital technology, including AI mental-health treatment and companion-related suicidal ideation and harm. Findings are due April 23, 2027; the commission expires May 28, 2027.
Healthcare Implications: Includes a child behavioral-health expert and an express healthcare-AI remit. Creates legislative study and recommendations, with no clinical duties or treatment authorization.
Stakeholder Tags: Patients & Public; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: G1: Advisory study commission or task force.
Specific Implications: The commission must examine AI mental-health treatment and possible regulation, and companion-related suicidal ideation or harm, then report to House Education by April 23, 2027.

Policy Name/Number: HB1139 – Use of Artificial Intelligence in Health Care
Summary: Regulates the use of artificial intelligence systems in utilization review for health-care services by carriers, pharmacy benefit managers, private utilization review organizations, behavioral health administrative services organizations, and managed care entities. Requires AI determinations to consider individual clinical context, prohibits sole reliance on group data, requires fair and nondiscriminatory application, periodic review, documentation and audit records, regulator disclosure, limits on secondary use of health data, and licensed human review before medical-necessity denials based in whole or part on AI output. Also prohibits covered payers from paying for psychotherapy services conducted directly by an AI system.
Healthcare Implications: Directly constrains payer, PBM, utilization-review, Medicaid, CHIP, and behavioral-health plan use of AI in coverage decisions. Covered entities must maintain human clinical oversight, document and disclose utilization-review AI use to regulators, preserve audit records, review AI performance, and avoid AI-only adverse medical-necessity decisions. Providers and patients gain protections against automated denials and against payer reimbursement for AI-conducted psychotherapy.

Policy Name/Number: HB475 – Artificial Intelligence Transcription Disclosure
Summary: Requires healthcare professionals licensed under Title 37 to verbally disclose the use of any recording device, software, or service before recording any part of an appointment or treatment for transcription by artificial intelligence. Violations may result in professional licensing-board discipline; the law provides civil immunity absent gross negligence or willful misconduct.
Healthcare Implications: Creates a patient-notice requirement for ambient AI scribes and other AI transcription tools used during clinical encounters. Licensed healthcare professionals must provide verbal notice before recording; the law does not require patient consent, an opt-out, or post-transcription accuracy review.
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: D2a: Healthcare practitioners must disclose to patients when using AI in their care.
Specific Implications: Before recording any part of an appointment or treatment for transcription by artificial intelligence, a healthcare professional licensed under Title 37 must verbally disclose the recording device, software, or service to the patient; violations may be disciplined by the applicable professional licensing board.

Policy Name/Number: HB1263 – Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service Operator Requirements
Summary: Establishes requirements for operators of publicly available conversational artificial intelligence services. Operators must disclose to users that the service is AI, use commercially reasonable or generally accepted methods to estimate user age, provide additional disclosures and safeguards for minors, restrict engagement incentives and harmful sexual or emotionally dependent outputs for minors, implement a suicide and self-harm response protocol, annually report protocol information to the Attorney General, and avoid representing AI outputs as provided by, endorsed by, or equivalent to services from licensed or certified professionals. Principal operator requirements begin January 1, 2027.
Healthcare Implications: The law is not healthcare-specific and excludes some HIPAA-covered and health-insurance contexts, but it is relevant to mental-health-adjacent conversational AI, AI companions, and consumer chatbots that may interact with minors or users expressing suicidal ideation or self-harm. Developers and operators of covered public-facing AI services must add disclosure, age-estimation, youth-safety, crisis-response, reporting, and professional-representation controls.

Policy Name/Number: SB386 – Consumer Data Privacy: Automated Decisions
Summary: Establishes consumer privacy protections, including opt-outs from solely automated profiling producing significant decisions about healthcare services. Requires data-protection assessments for specified risky processing.
Healthcare Implications: Covered health-related consumer services must assess applicable profiling and honor opt-out rights. HIPAA-covered entities and business associates, protected health information, and health records are exempt; the law does not generally require clinician review of AI decisions.
Stakeholder Tags: Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: P1: Internal procedures (impact assessments, periodic reviews, training) the deploying entity must maintain.
Specific Implications: Conduct and document assessments for profiling presenting specified foreseeable risks and other listed processing; make assessments available to the Attorney General on request.

Policy Name/Number: HF4188 – Automated Processing in Adverse Utilization Review Determinations
Summary: Prohibits utilization review organizations from using automated processing alone to make adverse clinical determinations. Requires clinician review by an appropriate health professional; physician reviewers generally must hold an unrestricted Minnesota license and have the same or a similar specialty as a provider who typically treats the condition. Prescription-drug determinations may be reviewed by a competent licensed pharmacist or physician.
Healthcare Implications: Requires covered health plans and utilization review organizations to keep qualified clinicians in the loop for adverse coverage decisions. Automated systems may support review but cannot independently deny care; the requirement applies to health plans offered, sold, issued, or renewed on or after January 1, 2027.
Keyword Tags: Safety & Risk; Transparency & Governance; Clinical Quality & Efficacy
Stakeholder Tags: Payers & Purchasers; Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: U1: Adverse coverage/claims/UR determinations may not be made solely by AI; a qualified human must make the final adverse decision.
Specific Implications: A utilization review organization may not make an adverse determination using automated processing alone; an appropriate clinician must review the determination, with physician reviewers generally licensed in Minnesota and practicing in the same or a similar specialty, and prescription-drug reviews performed by a competent licensed pharmacist or physician.

Policy Name/Number: SB1700 / HB1946 – TACIR AI Regulation and Mental Health Safeguards Study
Summary: Public Chapter 1082 directs TACIR to study potential AI and generative-chatbot regulation, including mental-health safeguards and suicide-prevention protocols, and publish recommendations.
Healthcare Implications: Creates a limited study of safeguards, constitutional constraints and economic impacts. It follows the distinct child-safety study under Chapter 1066, already represented by HB1455; it creates no chatbot treatment restrictions.
Stakeholder Tags: Regulators & Government; Patients & Public
Taxonomy Rules: G3: Directs a one-time agency study without rulemaking authority.
Specific Implications: TACIR must review AI regulation, including safeguards for minors and mental health and suicide-prevention protocols, and deliver a report to the governor, legislative speakers and librarian; no statutory report date remains.

Policy Name/Number: HB1455 – TACIR Artificial Intelligence Study
Summary: Requires the Tennessee Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Relations to study artificial intelligence and submit a report to the Governor and legislative speakers by January 31, 2027. The study must assess AI risks, mitigation methods, national and international standards, dangerous prompts such as suicide or violent-crime encouragement, and risks from AI chatbots engaging with users as human while providing emotional support, mental health care, or health care.
Healthcare Implications: Creates no direct operational obligations for healthcare providers, payers, or AI developers, but gives Tennessee a formal study process for AI chatbot risks involving mental health care and health care. The report may inform future state policy on AI companions, mental-health chatbots, health-related prompt safety, and AI systems that users may treat as human or therapeutic.

Policy Name/Number: H0814 – Neurological Rights and AI in Health and Human Services
Summary: Recognizes neurological rights and expands the AI Advisory Council’s membership and duration through June 30, 2030. Requires review of professional AI guidance and a January 15, 2027 report recommending further neurological-rights, regulated-profession and health-insurance utilization-review legislation.
Healthcare Implications: Creates a healthcare-AI policy study and recommendation process. The final act does not enact the patient-communication, mental-health-chatbot or insurer utilization-review operating duties described in the existing row.

Policy Name/Number: SB26-189 – Automated Decision-Making Technology
Summary: Replaces Colorado’s prior high-risk-AI framework with an automated decision-making technology law. General documentation, recordkeeping, notice and requested human-review requirements apply from January 1, 2027, subject to substantial exemptions. HIPAA-covered healthcare entities/business associates and qualifying insurers receive special treatment; covered healthcare entities retain patient notice and financial-assistance disclosure duties. Specified rulemaking and preparatory provisions took effect on passage.
Healthcare Implications: The general ADMT duties do not uniformly govern clinical care or health-insurance decisions. Section 6-1-1708 exempts HIPAA-covered entities and their business associates from specified general duties, except employment decisions, with an in-state-location condition for healthcare providers. Covered entities must give general advanced-technology notice and specified information for ADMT-assisted patient financial-assistance decisions. Qualifying insurers are deemed compliant in insurance practice; other insurers face applicable adverse-outcome disclosure. FDA-regulated devices and specified research are excluded.

Policy Name/Number: HF2635 – Health Carriers, Utilization Review, Artificial Intelligence, Audits, and Prior Authorizations
Summary: Amends Iowa health insurance and utilization review law to address health carrier standards of conduct, utilization review organization audits, prior authorizations, and AI use. The law allows utilization review organizations to use AI-based algorithms or systems for initial prior authorization review, but prohibits AI from serving as the sole basis for denying, delaying, or downgrading a medical-necessity prior authorization request. It also requires qualified reviewer or clinical peer involvement for prior-authorization denials or downgrades and sets provider notice, audit, appeal, and documentation requirements.
Healthcare Implications: Directly limits payer and utilization-review use of AI in prior authorization. AI can support initial review, but medical-necessity denials, delays, or downgrades must not be solely AI-based and must involve qualified clinical review with written reasons and appeal rights. The law affects health carriers, utilization review organizations, providers submitting prior authorization requests, covered persons, and the Iowa Insurance Commissioner.

Policy Name/Number: SB00005 – Public Act 26-15 – An Act Concerning Online Safety
Summary: Requires AI companion operators to implement suicide, self-harm, and imminent-violence protocols and provide disclosures that users are interacting with AI. Restricts provision of AI companions to minors when certain harmful, sexual, manipulative, or mental-health-service functions are reasonably foreseeable, with a narrow clinically supervised mental-health exception. Also directs the Office of Health Strategy to create a program using AI systems to enhance health outcomes, including de-identified health data pilots and an annual healthcare AI competition.
Healthcare Implications: Creates strong consumer and youth-safety obligations for AI companions with mental-health relevance, enforced by the Attorney General and private rights in certain minor-related contexts. Also gives Connecticut’s Office of Health Strategy a formal role in health AI innovation using de-identified health data, making the law relevant both to behavioral-health chatbot safety and state-supported healthcare AI pilots.

Policy Name/Number: SB540 – AI Companion Chatbot Safety
Summary: Regulates operators of AI companion chatbots that use AI, generative AI, or emotional-recognition algorithms to simulate sustained human or human-like relationships with users. Requires recurring disclosure that users are interacting with AI, heightened protections for minors, crisis-response protocols for severe harm and eating-disorder-related self-harm, public protocol disclosures and annual crisis-referral metrics, age-assurance for sexually explicit synthetic-content features, privacy limits for age-assurance data, and Attorney General enforcement.
Healthcare Implications: Directly affects mental-health-adjacent AI companion tools and consumer AI systems that may be used for emotional support, crisis conversations, or simulated therapeutic relationships. Operators must build disclosure, minor-safety, crisis-routing, privacy, and escalation workflows, and may not knowingly represent that an AI companion chatbot is licensed or authorized to provide mental health, behavioral health, medical, or counseling services unless lawfully authorized.

Policy Name/Number: SB444 – Private Review Agents; Artificial Intelligence in Insurance Coverage Decisions
Summary: Amends Georgia’s private review agent and utilization review framework to permit appropriate use of artificial intelligence, artificial intelligence systems, and software tools while prohibiting certain healthcare insurance coverage decisions from being based solely on those tools. Requires natural-person utilization review with clinical peer participation before adverse determinations and preserves clinical peer judgment.
Healthcare Implications: Directly constrains payer and utilization-review use of AI for medical-necessity or coverage decisions. Private review agents, utilization review entities, and payers using AI must keep qualified human review and clinical peer participation in the adverse-determination workflow, while regulators retain oversight through Georgia’s existing private review agent and utilization review framework.

Policy Name/Number: SF2417 – Conversational AI Services
Summary: Establishes requirements for operators of publicly accessible conversational AI services, including AI-human disclosure duties, special safeguards for minor users, suicide and self-harm response protocols, a restriction on representing conversational AI as providing licensed psychology or behavioral health services, attorney general rulemaking/enforcement authority, and civil penalties. It is relevant to developers/operators of consumer AI companions or chatbots that could interact with patients, minors, or users seeking behavioral-health support.

Summary: Authorizes the Insurance Commissioner to examine patterns of emergency-department adverse decisions and obtain independent review at the carrier’s expense. Adds post-acute reporting and facility studies; existing carrier reports already identify AI-assisted adverse decisions.

Policy Name/Number: SCR184 – Requesting the Hawaii Civil Rights Commission to Examine Algorithmic Decision Systems
Summary: Requests the Hawaii Civil Rights Commission to examine how existing anti-discrimination laws apply to algorithmic and automated decision systems and to assess risks of bias and disparate impact.

Policy Name/Number: HB191 – Medical Professionals, Titles, and Nonhuman Entities
Summary: Amends Delaware health-professional licensing laws to clarify that nonhuman entities, including agents powered by artificial intelligence, may not be licensed as professional nurses, advanced practice registered nurses, practical nurses, physicians, or physician assistants and may not use protected nursing, physician, or physician-assistant titles and abbreviations.

Health systems and vendors should avoid interfaces, marketing, or automated communications that imply an AI system is a licensed nurse, physician, doctor, medical doctor, doctor of osteopathy, surgeon, or physician assistant.

Summary: Prohibits developing or deploying an AI system that advertises or represents to the public that it is, or can act as, a qualified mental health professional. Violations trigger consumer-protection enforcement.

Policy Name/Number: HB2155 – Nursing Titles: Nonhuman Entities
Summary: Bars nonhuman entities from using protected nursing titles or representations indicating nursing licensure. Amends registered, advanced-practice, and licensed-practical nursing title protections.

Policy Name/Number: HB0102 – AI Systems Intended to Promote Self-Harm
Summary: Creates a felony for knowingly developing or distributing AI specifically designed to promote self-harm, with the required intent or knowledge. The wider act also addresses synthetic sexual material, criminal liability and limited developer immunity.
Healthcare Implications: Adds a targeted self-harm safety restriction relevant to mental-health-facing AI developers and distributors. It creates no general crisis-response protocol.

Summary: Prohibits certain downcoding practices in health insurance claims and restricts the use of automated processes, systems, or tools, including artificial intelligence, in claim submission and adjudication without appropriate review.
Healthcare Implications: Would directly impact payer and provider use of AI in claims processing by limiting automated downcoding and requiring human oversight in utilization management workflows. Policy Name/Number: S07599 / S07543 – Legislative Oversight of Automated Decision-Making in Government Act (LOADinG Act)
Summary: Regulates automated decision-making systems used by New York government agencies through meaningful human review, periodic impact assessments, bias/privacy/cybersecurity/public-health risk review, and public disclosure of agency ADM tools. Policy Name/Number: S06953 / S8828 – Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act
Summary: Requires large frontier-model developers to create and publish safety plans, run risk assessments, report significant safety incidents, and comply with state oversight. Policy Name/Number: SB243 – Companion Chatbots
Summary: Requires conditional AI disclosure, published suicide/self-harm safeguards, and annual reporting beginning July 1, 2027. SB1119 removes the original minor-specific subsection effective January 1, 2027 and introduces a separate phased child-safety framework.

Policy Name/Number: AB979 – California Cybersecurity Integration Center: Artificial Intelligence
Summary: Directs the California Cybersecurity Integration Center, working with the Office of Information Security and the Government Operations Agency, to publish by January 1, 2027 a California AI Cybersecurity Collaboration Playbook coordinating threat and vulnerability information-sharing across cyber and AI communities. Requires state AI contractors to share relevant threats with a designated state entity and protects shared indicators from disclosure under the California Public Records Act.

Summary: Regulates frontier (highly advanced, large-scale, general-purpose) models and their large developers. Policy Name/Number: HB1806 – Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act
Summary: Creates the Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act, prohibiting any person or company from using AI to provide therapy or psychotherapy or to make therapeutic decisions. Licensed professionals may still use AI for administrative or supplementary support (e.g., scheduling, billing, record management) but not for diagnosis or treatment. The Act authorizes enforcement by the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation and includes specified exceptions (e.g., religious counseling, peer support, self‑help materials).
Healthcare Implications: Bars AI chatbots and similar tools from acting as therapists or conducting therapy in Illinois, tightening clinical safety and accountability. Behavioral health providers must ensure any AI deployed is confined to administrative support and maintain human clinical judgment for care. Vendors marketing AI therapy or decision‑making tools face enforcement risk; procurement and compliance teams should update contracts and disclosures.

Summary: Directs Delaware’s Artificial Intelligence Commission, in collaboration with the Secretary of State, to develop a proposed framework for an agentic AI regulatory sandbox and report back with recommendations. It does not itself create or launch a sandbox program.

Policy Name/Number: HB3936 – Restriction on AI from Covered Vendors

Policy Name/Number: SB815 – Automated Systems in Health Benefit Claims Process
Summary: Regulates the use of certain automated systems, including algorithms that incorporate artificial intelligence, in the health benefit claims process and utilization review. Defines “artificial intelligence system” and “automated decision system” in the Insurance Code, and prohibits a utilization review agent from using an automated decision system to make, wholly or partly, an adverse determination about medical necessity or coverage. Applies to plans delivered, issued for delivery, or renewed on or after January 1, 2026.

The commissioner may inspect and audit system use at any time. Adverse notices must state reasons, clinical basis, screening/review criteria and appeal procedures; the Act does not itself require a notice that AI was used.

Policy Name/Number: SB1188 – Electronic Health Record Requirements
Summary: Sets requirements for electronic health records maintained by covered entities in Texas. Policy Name/Number: LD1727 – AI Chatbot Disclosure in Consumer Transactions
Summary: Requires businesses and other persons that use artificial intelligence chatbots in trade or commerce to clearly disclose to consumers when they are interacting with a non-human system, prohibiting the use of AI chatbots or similar technologies in a manner that misleads a reasonable consumer into believing they are communicating with a human and treating violations as unfair trade practices enforceable by the Attorney General.

Summary: Enacts restrictions on AI in mental and behavioral health: bars AI providers and unlicensed persons from representing AI systems as capable of providing professional mental/behavioral healthcare; prohibits offering AI that is programmed to deliver such care; and limits provider use of AI to administrative support (e.g., scheduling, billing, operational analytics). Policy Name/Number: HB820 – Health Insurance – Utilization Review - Use of Artificial Intelligence
Summary: Regulates AI, algorithms and software used for utilization review by carriers and contracted PBMs/private review agents. Tools must use individual clinical information, avoid group-data-only decisions and discrimination, support regulator inspection and documented oversight, undergo at-least-quarterly review, and respect patient-data purpose limits. Such tools may not deny, delay or modify health-care services.
Healthcare Implications: Covered payers and review entities must preserve provider decision-making, prevent software-driven denials/delays/modifications, maintain and file AI oversight policies, permit Commissioner audits and report AI use in adverse decisions. Patient data has a purpose limitation; the law does not create a general patient AI-disclosure duty.
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Regulators & Government

Policy Name/Number: HB2175 – Prior Authorization; Claims

Summary: Operative law under New York General Business Law Article 47, enacted through the 2025 state budget, requiring disclosure for personalized algorithmic pricing and establishing safeguards for AI companions, including crisis-response protocols and clear notices that users are interacting with AI.
Healthcare Implications: Direct implications for mental health and digital wellness tools that function as AI companions: systems must detect suicidal ideation/self-harm cues and route users to crisis services, which shapes how mental-health and wellness apps marketed in NY design, monitor, and govern AI companion features.

Policy Name/Number: HB178 – Limit Government Use of AI Systems
Summary: Restricts state/local government uses of AI, prohibiting cognitive behavioral manipulation, discriminatory classification, and broad public‑space surveillance (with narrow exceptions). Requires disclosure when agencies use AI in public‑facing tools or publish unreviewed AI content, and mandates human review for AI outputs that affect rights or duties.

AI cannot be the sole basis for determinations impacting individuals. Limits on public‑space surveillance may curb live‑video analytics in health/public‑safety contexts.

Policy Name/Number: SB2280 – Prior Authorization Reform Act
Summary: Prior-authorization reform requiring qualified clinical review, appeal procedures, published criteria, and reporting. The bill does not explicitly mention artificial intelligence, automated decision systems, or algorithms.

Summary: Establishes the Workgroup on Artificial Intelligence Implementation within the Office of the Attorney General to study AI’s consumer‑protection implications, current private‑sector uses, enforcement authority, and impacts on government‑benefits determinations, and to report recommendations to the General Assembly by July 1, 2026.

Summary: Directs a legislative interim study of AI, including a survey of Montana, other state, and federal laws; exploration of an AI code of ethics and potential bill of rights; and analysis of transparency/disclosure requirements and civil/criminal liability for AI developers and deployers.

Policy Name/Number: HB1876 – Regarding the Ownership of Model Training and Content Generated by a Generative Artificial Intelligence Tool
Summary: Clarifies ownership of content generated by generative AI tools and certain model-training outputs, including work-for-hire exceptions and contractual allocation of rights.

Policy Name/Number: HB1958 – To Require Public Entities to Create a Policy Concerning the Authorized Use of Artificial Intelligence
Summary: Requires Arkansas public entities (state agencies, local governments, public schools, and higher-ed) to adopt an AI/automated decision tool policy that defines authorized uses, ensures human-in-the-loop review, and documents oversight. Policy Name/Number: SB212 – Right to Compute Act
Summary: Protects the right to use personal computational resources while including AI-related provisions relevant to risk management and critical-infrastructure contexts.

Policy Name/Number: HB178 – Nursing Practice Changes
Summary: Amends the New Mexico Nursing Practice Act to clarify nursing scope and Board of Nursing powers, including authority for the Board to promulgate rules on the use of artificial intelligence in nursing.

Policy Name/Number: SR391 – Senate Study Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Digital Currency
Summary: Creates the Senate Study Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Digital Currency to examine policy impacts, risks, and opportunities across Georgia’s economy, including public services. The committee is tasked with hearings and recommendations for the 2025–2026 biennium.

Policy Name/Number: HB0452 – Artificial Intelligence Amendments

Summary: Requires California state agencies to report on and disclose specified uses of generative AI, directs updates to statewide GenAI reporting, requires analysis of GenAI risks to critical infrastructure, and embeds portions of the Governor’s AI executive order into statute.

Policy Name/Number: SB1120 – Physicians Make Decisions Act
Summary: Regulates payors’ use of AI and automated decision tools in utilization management by requiring qualified clinical decision-making, individual clinical-context review, fairness and non-discrimination, auditability, written AI oversight policies, periodic review, limits on secondary patient-data use, and protections against AI-related harm.

Health plans and insurers must keep human clinical oversight over medical-necessity decisions, prevent discriminatory or group-data-only determinations, make AI policies available, support regulator audits, limit patient-data reuse, and avoid AI practices that harm enrollees.

Policy Name/Number: AB3030 – Health Care Services: Artificial Intelligence
Summary: Requires health facilities, clinics, and physician/group practices that use generative AI to generate written or verbal patient communications about clinical information to include both (1) a disclaimer indicating AI was used and (2) clear instructions for how the patient can reach a human clinician/staff. Communications read and reviewed by a human licensed or certified healthcare provider are exempt; violations by physicians are subject to Medical Board/Osteopathic Board jurisdiction.
Healthcare Implications: Directly impacts patient‑facing chatbots, portal messages, automated call scripts, and discharge instructions, mandating transparency and human‑escalation pathways. Drives changes to vendor contracts, quality assurance, and risk management for generative AI in care delivery. Supports patient comprehension and informed consent by clarifying when AI assists in clinical communications.

Taxonomy Rules: D2a: Healthcare practitioners must disclose to patients when using AI in their care.

Exempt if the communication is read and reviewed by a human licensed or certified healthcare provider. Physician violations subject to Medical Board jurisdiction.

Policy Name/Number: AB2885 – Artificial Intelligence
Summary: Creates a uniform definition of “artificial intelligence” across multiple California codes and directs the Government Operations Agency and Department of Technology to coordinate planning around deepfakes and AI risks. Supports statewide risk assessment of AI/Automated Decision System used by government programs that interact with healthcare (e.g., eligibility, fraud, benefits). Sets groundwork for future health‑specific AI guidance to align to a shared baseline.

Policy Name/Number: AB1282 – Mental Health: Impacts of Social Media
Summary: Requires the Department of Public Health, in consultation with the Mental Health Services Oversight and Accountability Commission, to deliver by Dec. 31, 2026 a statewide strategy to understand, communicate, and mitigate youth mental‑health risks associated with social media. Policy Name/Number: SB1223 – Consumer Privacy: Sensitive Personal Information: Neural Data
Summary: Defines “neural data” (e.g., EEG/fMRI/BCI signals, eye‑tracking, neural recordings) as Sensitive Personal Information under the California Consumer Privacy Act. Extends CCPA rights and duties to neural data–right to know/limit/opt‑out, purpose limitation, and reasonable security–and prohibits selling or sharing neural data without opt‑in consent except as permitted by law.
Healthcare Implications: Neurotechnology, mental‑health apps, and medical devices that collect brain‑signal or neuro‑adjacent data must treat it as highly protected SPI, tightening consent and limiting secondary uses (e.g., AI training) outside Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. Providers and vendors integrating BCIs or neuro‑monitoring need new data‑governance controls and contractual terms for third‑party analytics. Raises compliance expectations for de‑identification and security when neural data are combined with other patient information.
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems

Policy Name/Number: AB2013 – Generative Artificial Intelligence: Training Data Transparency

Summary: Requires large generative-AI providers to support content provenance and disclosure for AI-generated image, video, and audio content, including detection tools and manifest/latent disclosures.

Policy Name/Number: HB1688 – Use of AI by State Agencies
Summary: Creates RSA 5‑D governing AI use by state agencies: requires transparency when the public interacts with AI, mandates human review for significant decisions, and establishes guardrails on biometric identification/surveillance. Includes definitions and agency governance duties.
Healthcare Implications: Public‑sector health programs using AI (e.g., eligibility chatbots, triage, fraud analytics) must disclose AI use and add human review for impactful determinations. Restrictions on real‑time biometric ID limit live facial recognition uses in health/public safety contexts. Agencies must conduct risk assessments and implement governance when procuring AI health tools.
Stakeholder Tags: Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors
Taxonomy Rules: H2: Consequential AI-driven decisions affecting individuals' rights, benefits, or welfare require human review before taking effect. | D1: AI systems must disclose their non-human nature when interacting directly with users. | E1: AI systems must be evaluated for discriminatory or biased outcomes; entities must take specified action if discrimination is found. | P2: Deploying entities must publicly disclose or file with regulators detailed information about their AI systems, policies, or inventories.
Specific Implications: Irreversible AI-generated recommendations or decisions affecting rights, biometric ID, critical infrastructure, law enforcement, or legal interpretation must be reviewed by a trained human aware of the AI's limitations. | AI interactions with users must be disclosed; generative AI material not human-reviewed must include AI disclosure. | Prohibits AI classification of persons resulting in unlawful discrimination. | Within 9 months, all state agencies must review AI use and report to DoIT; DoIT publishes annual report on agency AI systems on its website.

Policy Name/Number: HR170 – Directing the Joint State Government Commission to Establish an Advisory Committee...
Summary: Directs the Pennsylvania Joint State Government Commission to establish an advisory committee to study artificial intelligence and make recommendations on AI governance, oversight, and responsible public-sector use.
Healthcare Implications: May inform Pennsylvania state-agency AI governance, including agencies or programs connected to Medicaid, public health, licensing, and benefits administration. It does not impose direct healthcare AI obligations, but it could shape future standards for transparency, accountability, and human oversight in public-sector health programs.
Stakeholder Tags: Regulators & Government; Providers & Health Systems; Developers & Vendors
Taxonomy Rules: G1: Advisory study commission or task force.
Specific Implications: Directs the Joint State Government Commission to establish an advisory committee and study AI, including responsible growth, state-government use, other states’ regulation, and recommendations for legislation. The committee includes the Secretary of Health and a Pennsylvania Medical Society representative. Report due within 18 months after adoption; the current legislative record links the completed report. This is a legislative study, not a directive to implement the Governor’s AI executive order.

Policy Name/Number: HF4757 / Chapter 121, Article 5 – Minnesota Consumer Data Privacy Act
Summary: Creates rights to opt out of consequential profiling, question and obtain reasons for profiling results, review underlying personal data, and obtain reevaluation when inaccurate data is corrected. Significant decisions expressly include health-care services; specified risky processing requires data-protection assessments.
Healthcare Implications: Covered nonexempt health-related controllers must honor applicable profiling rights and assessment duties. HIPAA-protected information, health records, other exempt clinical data, and insurance companies remain outside coverage. Reevaluation after correcting inaccurate data is not a right to clinician review of a clinical decision.
Stakeholder Tags: Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: P1: Internal procedures (impact assessments, periodic reviews, training) the deploying entity must maintain.
Specific Implications: Covered controllers must conduct and document assessments for profiling presenting specified foreseeable risks and other covered processing; provide relevant assessments to the Attorney General on request.

Policy Name/Number: SB818 – Artificial Intelligence Governance Act of 2024
Summary: Requires each unit of Maryland state government to inventory AI systems; conduct impact assessments; and, under the Department of Information Technology, adopt policies and procedures governing the development, procurement, deployment, use, and assessment of AI.
Healthcare Implications: Applies to state health entities (e.g., MDH, Medicaid) that operate AI‑enabled systems in eligibility, program integrity, and public‑health analytics. Expect standardized inventories, risk assessments, and governance processes that vendors must satisfy when contracting with the state.
Stakeholder Tags: Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: P2: Deploying entities must publicly disclose or file with regulators detailed information about their AI systems, policies, or inventories. | G2: Directs an agency to issue binding rules, standards, or regulatory guidance on AI. | G1: Advisory study commission or task force.
Specific Implications: Each unit of state government must conduct inventories and impact assessments of high-risk AI systems. | DoIT directed to adopt policies and procedures for development, procurement, deployment, use, and assessment of state AI systems. | Establishes Governor's AI Subcabinet; develops roadmap; submits reports to Governor and General Assembly.

Policy Name/Number: SB487 – JCOTS study on AI use by public bodies
Summary: Directs the Joint Commission on Technology and Science to examine and provide recommendations on the use of artificial intelligence by public bodies; authorizes study, reporting, and coordination with agencies.
Healthcare Implications: Virginia health agencies and public hospitals fall within the scope of JCOTS’ examination. Expect future standards on transparency, inventories, and human oversight for AI used in benefits, licensing, and public‑health programs.
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Developers & Vendors
Taxonomy Rules: G3: Directs a one-time agency study without rulemaking authority.
Specific Implications: Directs JCOTS to examine and recommend on AI use by public bodies; authorizes study, reporting, and coordination with agencies.

Policy Name/Number: SB7018 – Health Care Innovation Council and Revolving Loan Program
Summary: Creates the Health Care Innovation Council within the Department of Health and establishes a revolving loan program to scale promising health innovations statewide. The Council advises on priorities and oversees annual reporting.
Healthcare Implications: AI‑enabled solutions (clinical decision support, imaging triage, virtual care, revenue cycle automation) can qualify for technical assistance and financing, accelerating adoption by hospitals and community providers. Expect pilots to require outcome tracking, privacy/security compliance, and equitable access considerations to receive support.
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Developers & Vendors
Taxonomy Rules: G1: Advisory study commission or task force.
Specific Implications: Creates Health Care Innovation Council within DOH; establishes revolving loan program for health innovations. Not AI-specific but health-innovation focused.

Policy Name/Number: SB5838 – Establishing an Artificial Intelligence Task Force
Summary: Creates a statewide Artificial Intelligence Task Force to study AI uses and risks across sectors; requires recommendations on governance, transparency, and workforce impacts.
Healthcare Implications: Health stakeholders are included among sectors to be consulted, with implications for standards around clinical decision support, patient communications, and equity in AI deployment in Washington.
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Developers & Vendors
Taxonomy Rules: G1: Advisory study commission or task force.
Specific Implications: Creates statewide AI Task Force to study AI uses and risks; requires recommendations on governance, transparency, and workforce impacts.

Policy Name/Number: SB0149 – Artificial Intelligence Amendments
Summary: Enacts Utah’s AI consumer-protection framework, including liability and disclosure rules for generative-AI interactions, an Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy and an AI Learning Laboratory regulatory program. Later amendments, including SB226, narrow specified disclosure triggers.
Healthcare Implications: Regulated healthcare professionals and covered suppliers must assess applicable consumer-interaction disclosure rules. The original Act’s regulated-occupation notice was narrowed by SB226 to high-risk interactions; the Act also creates a regulatory learning-laboratory pathway. It does not generally impose the state-health procurement or universal human-review duties implied by the original implications.
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors
Taxonomy Rules: D1: AI systems must disclose their non-human nature when interacting directly with users. | D2a: Healthcare practitioners must disclose to patients when using AI in their care. | G2: Directs an agency to issue binding rules, standards, or regulatory guidance on AI.
Specific Implications: GenAI in non-regulated consumer transaction must disclose AI nature when consumer asks (narrowed in 2025 to 'clear and unambiguous request'). | Regulated occupations (including healthcare professions) must prominently disclose GenAI use at outset of interaction (narrowed in 2025 by SB0226 to 'high-risk AI interactions' only). | Office of AI Policy with rulemaking authority; AI Learning Laboratory Program (regulatory sandbox).

Policy Name/Number: SB0150 – Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity
Summary: Creates the Indiana Artificial Intelligence Task Force to study and assess the use of AI by state agencies and to recommend policies on technology resources and cybersecurity. Authorizes public entities to adopt technology and cybersecurity policies, directs inventories of AI technologies in use, and clarifies state software licensing oversight.
Healthcare Implications: Indiana’s health agencies and state-run health programs must inventory and evaluate AI tools (e.g., triage chatbots, predictive analytics, fraud detection) and align with statewide cybersecurity requirements. Task Force guidance can shape procurement criteria for Electronic Health Record add‑ons, decision‑support software, and vendor risk management.
Stakeholder Tags: Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: G1: Advisory study commission or task force. | P2: Deploying entities must publicly disclose or file with regulators detailed information about their AI systems, policies, or inventories.
Specific Implications: Creates Indiana AI Task Force to study and assess AI use by state agencies. | Directs inventories of AI technologies in use by public entities. One of few task-force bills with an actual operative inventory provision.

Policy Name/Number: HB5690 – Creating a West Virginia Task Force on Artificial Intelligence
Summary: Creates the West Virginia Task Force on Artificial Intelligence within the Office of Technology; sets membership, duties (including a report), and a termination date.
Healthcare Implications: Task force scope includes examining AI’s impacts on public services and the workforce, relevant to public hospitals and health programs. Expect recommendations that influence procurement, transparency, and risk management for AI used in state‑connected health systems.
Stakeholder Tags: Providers & Health Systems; Developers & Vendors
Taxonomy Rules: G1: Advisory study commission or task force.
Specific Implications: Creates WV Task Force on AI within Office of Technology; sets membership, duties, reporting, and termination date.

Policy Name/Number: HR3 – Creating a Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence
Summary: House Resolution creating a Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence for the remainder of the 86th Legislature to study AI issues and recommend action to the Speaker.
Healthcare Implications: Signals legislative attention to AI impacts across sectors, including healthcare delivery and patient data. Provides a venue for stakeholder input that may shape future AI guardrails affecting providers and payers.
Stakeholder Tags: Regulators & Government; Providers & Health Systems; Payers & Purchasers
Taxonomy Rules: G1: Advisory study commission or task force.
Specific Implications: Creates Select Committee on AI for the 86th Legislature to study AI issues and recommend action.

Policy Name/Number: AB302 – Department of Technology: High-Risk Automated Decision Systems: Inventory
Summary: Directs the California Department of Technology to inventory high-risk automated decision systems used, developed, or proposed by state agencies, including specified healthcare decisions, and report the inventory annually to legislative committees. The inventory describes existing safeguards and processes; the Act does not itself impose a general requirement to adopt risk-management policies.
Healthcare Implications: Covers Automated Decision System deployed by state health entities (e.g., Medi‑Cal eligibility, program integrity, triage), increasing transparency into government AI that affects access to care and benefits. Encourages bias testing and accountability measures that health providers and advocacy groups can monitor. May influence procurement standards for AI tools interfacing with public health and human services programs.
Stakeholder Tags: Payers & Purchasers; Regulators & Government
Taxonomy Rules: P2: Deploying entities must publicly disclose or file with regulators detailed information about their AI systems, policies, or inventories.
Specific Implications: Department of Technology must conduct comprehensive inventory of all high-risk ADM systems used/proposed by state agencies (decisions, alternatives, efficacy research, data categories, mitigation measures); annual report to Legislature. 'High-risk' defined to include healthcare decisions.

Policy Name/Number: SB01103 – An Act Concerning Artificial Intelligence, Automated Decision-Making and Personal Data Privacy
Summary: Establishes an Office of Artificial Intelligence; requires annual inventories of AI systems used by executive and judicial branches; mandates policies and procedures for state agency AI development, procurement, use, and assessments; and amends the state privacy law (including teen targeted‑ads limits).
Healthcare Implications: Covers AI governance for state health agencies (e.g., DSS, DPH), including risk assessment, transparency, and bias mitigation for automated systems that can affect benefits eligibility, licensing, or other health‑related decisions. A reference point for hospital compliance teams engaging with state systems.
Keyword Tags: Transparency & Governance; Privacy & Data; Equity & Bias; Safety & Risk
Stakeholder Tags: Regulators & Government; Patients & Public; Developers & Vendors; Providers & Health Systems
